reference.source: RCOG guidance on liver disease in pregnancy / Williams Obstetrics
clinicalPearls: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening microvesicular fatty infiltration of hepatocytes, typically presenting in the third trimester or early postpartum period

It is associated in a proportion of cases with inherited fetal defects of mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, especially long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, so testing of the newborn is warranted
Early symptoms are non-specific, including nausea, vomiting, anorexia, malaise, abdominal pain, and thirst or polyuria, progressing to jaundice and features of acute liver failure

Characteristic laboratory findings include hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with prolonged clotting times and low fibrinogen, raised transaminases and bilirubin, hyperuricaemia, renal impairment, and often a raised white cell count
The Swansea criteria provide a helpful clinical framework for diagnosis when a constellation of features is present and other causes are excluded
Hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy are hallmarks that help distinguish it from HELLP, although the two can overlap and coexist

Management is prompt delivery once the mother is stabilised, with intensive supportive care correcting hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, and electrolyte disturbance and managing hepatic and renal failure, occasionally requiring referral to a liver unit
It demands a high index of suspicion, as delay markedly worsens maternal and fetal outcome
reference.pathophysiology: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy reflects impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation within hepatocytes, leading to accumulation of microvesicular fat. In many cases the fetus carries a defect of the fatty-acid oxidation pathway, most notably long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; the metabolic burden of unmetabolised fatty-acid intermediates from the feto-placental unit is thought to overwhelm the maternal liver, whose oxidative capacity is already stressed in late pregnancy. The resulting hepatocellular dysfunction impairs gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycaemia; synthesis of clotting factors and fibrinogen, causing coagulopathy; and ureagenesis and clearance, causing hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy. Accumulation of toxic metabolites and endothelial dysfunction contribute to renal impairment and, in severe cases, multiorgan failure. Removal of the fetal and placental metabolic load by delivery allows the maternal liver to recover.
additionalDifferentials: Viral hepatitis, including hepatitis E, and other acute hepatitides
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Fulminant hepatic failure of another cause
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin, together with serum ammonia
Blood glucose, since hypoglycaemia is characteristic and needs frequent monitoring
Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and a full blood count
Viral hepatitis serology and other tests to exclude alternative causes
Liver ultrasound, chiefly to exclude other pathology such as a haematoma or Budd-Chiari syndrome
Neonatal screening for fatty-acid oxidation disorders after delivery
redFlags: Hepatic encephalopathy or a rising ammonia
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or major haemorrhage
Rapid clinical deterioration or fetal compromise
reference.prognosis: With early recognition, prompt delivery, and intensive supportive care, maternal survival and hepatic recovery are usual, though maternal and perinatal mortality remain significant when diagnosis is delayed; the liver typically recovers without long-term sequelae, and recurrence is uncommon but recognised, particularly with fatty-acid oxidation defects.
pitfalls: Dismissing late-pregnancy nausea and vomiting as benign and missing early disease
Failing to check and repeatedly monitor the blood glucose
Confusing it with HELLP and overlooking the coagulopathy and hypoglycaemia that guide management
Delaying delivery while awaiting confirmatory tests
Not arranging neonatal metabolic screening for fatty-acid oxidation disorders
references: RCOG guidance on liver disease in pregnancy
Oxford Handbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
management: Prompt delivery of the foetus as the definitive treatment once the mother is stabilised, regardless of gestation
Maternal stabilisation with intensive supportive care, including correction of hypoglycaemia by dextrose infusion
Correction of coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate and vitamin K
Management of acute liver failure complications, monitoring for hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy, with liver transplantation reserved for irreversible failure
Coordinated multidisciplinary care involving obstetrics, hepatology, intensive care and neonatology
Screening of the newborn for fatty-acid oxidation defects, particularly long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
Genetic counselling and discussion of the recurrence risk in future pregnancies
